## Q1 — Prune exposition without touching the falsification core

My read: the directive is not “mostly fluff,” but it is heavily over-narrated. The largest savings are not from deleting whole mechanisms; they are from stripping provenance, motivation, repeated explanation, and “why this exists” paragraphs from otherwise operative sections. I would be conservative on anything that affects parser compliance, tool receipts, admissibility, lifecycle, feedback, and alternatives.

### Section-by-section verdict

| Section | Verdict | Reason / proposed prune |
|---|---:|---|
| Preamble: “CDSFL Operational Directive…” | **COMPRESS** | Keep one sentence: “Follow this as the working protocol; tools decide truth where runnable.” Cut “operationalises model / formal notation” narration. Saving: ~250–300 chars. |
| §1 Falsification Protocol | **KEEP** | Core. Off-limits. |
| §2 What Your Output Must Contain | **KEEP** | Core output format. Off-limits, though I note the “runnable-falsifier block” is not actually very runnable as written. Still KEEP. |
| §3 Self-Assessment Equation | **KEEP** | Core. Off-limits. |
| §4 Break-Even Threshold | **KEEP** | Operative reject rule. Also mathematical; out of pruning scope except possibly later if founder permits. |
| §5 Marginal Gain and Stopping | **KEEP / tiny COMPRESS** | Mostly lean and operational. Could save ~100 chars by removing explanatory phrasing, but not worth risking ambiguity. |
| §6 Self-Assessment in Practice | **KEEP** | Core worked R procedure. Off-limits. |
| §7 Fix Format | **KEEP** | Core. Off-limits. |
| §7.1 Finding Lifecycle | **COMPRESS** | Operative FSM should stay. Cut Bugzilla analogy, “loop closure” explanation, and motivational convergence prose. Keep states, transition conditions, settled-finding rules, and closure via verified SEARCH/REPLACE. Saving: ~700–1,000 chars. |
| §8 Discovery Efficiency and Depletion | **COMPRESS** | Keep definitions and action bands for ρ and γ. Cut explanatory commentary about “well running dry” / “contributing new information” where redundant. Do not alter gamma. Saving: ~400–600 chars. |
| §8.1 Semantic Novelty | **COMPRESS** | Keep “semantic similarity detects duplicate root causes; high novelty continue; low novelty change approach; novelty does not bypass falsification.” Cut rest. Saving: ~300–450 chars. |
| §8.2 Suspicious Fast Convergence | **COMPRESS** | Important because it enforces “not model votes.” But it is over-explained. Keep signals and required action: flag fast model agreement as shared-prior risk unless tool/human verified. Saving: ~500–700 chars. |
| §9 Substrate Ceiling | **COMPRESS** | Keep hard exit condition and ν notation warning. Cut “not an intelligence generator” motivational paragraph if desired. Saving: ~250–400 chars. |
| §10 Proportionality | **KEEP / COMPRESS** | Operationally useful. Could be reduced to decision rule: full protocol for consequential non-obvious claims; light check for elementary/mechanically verified claims. Saving: ~250 chars. |
| §11 Constraint Classification | **KEEP** | Core. Off-limits. |
| §12 Epistemic Marking | **KEEP** | Core. Off-limits. |
| §13 Per-Round Operational Data | **CUT or MERGE** | Mostly duplicates §8 and registry instructions in §7.1. If §8 is retained compressed, §13 can be deleted wholesale or reduced to one line: “Use provided γ, ρ, ρ̄₃ and registry state to avoid redundant submissions.” Saving: ~600–700 chars. |
| §14 Modular vs Monolithic Falsification | **COMPRESS** | Keep rule: for 3+ independent components, do modular passes plus cross-cutting pass; otherwise monolithic. Cut “structural not cognitive” explanation and examples. Saving: ~400–550 chars. |
| §15 FFAFP | **KEEP** | Core. Off-limits. I would privately compress history/experiment provenance, but constraint says KEEP. |
| §16 Stage 6 Literature-Calibrated Extension | **COMPRESS** | Substantial operative content: η decomposition, triple report, orthogonality, reduction property. Cut Hossenfelder anecdote, table if replaced by one sentence, e-value shadow-mode unless active in current run, derivation/provenance paragraph, “Stage 5 special case” repetition. Saving: ~2,000–2,800 chars. |
| §17 Feedback Channel | **COMPRESS** | Mechanism is load-bearing, but wording is narrative. Keep schema feedback obligation, four flag types, resubmission rule, tool-receipt rule, rendering cap, disablement flag if relevant. Cut history, “entire point” prose, implementation paths, repeated “tools not infallible” explanation. Saving: ~1,500–2,200 chars. |
| §18 Divergence Directive | **COMPRESS, not CUT** | Largest bloat, but not just exposition: alternatives, contrast statement, dimensions, near-duplicate rules, channel assignment, hard-constraint interaction, feedback interaction are operative. Cut Popper-arm motivation, “round-2 unanimous review,” implementation paths, ratification history, repeated orthogonality prose, disablement rationale. Convert validator thresholds into a compact checklist. Saving: ~3,000–4,500 chars. |

### Rough total saving

Conservative savings: **~10k–13k chars** from a 44k-char directive, without touching the declared core.

More aggressive but still plausible: **~15k–17k chars**, mainly by compressing §§16–18 and deleting/merging §13. I would not promise more without risking behavioural loss, because §§17–18 are verbose but materially operative.

### Missing load-bearing pieces

1. **Explicit tool/human escalation rule.** The founding rule says truth is decided by tools, and where tools cannot decide, by humans — never model votes. The directive implies this but should state it operationally: “If no runnable check can decide the claim, mark NEEDS_HUMAN; do not resolve by panel agreement.”

2. **Actual runnable-falsifier schema.** §2 asks for FALSIFIER / ATTEMPT / RESULT, but not a concrete command, test snippet, input, expected failure, or reproducibility block. If the parser expects a “runnable-falsifier block,” the directive does not clearly define one.

3. **Tool receipt minimum.** Several sections demand tool output, but there is no uniform receipt schema: tool name, version, command/invocation, input, output excerpt, pass/fail mapping. This omission weakens tool-decidability.

4. **No-tools condition.** The model needs an admissible way to say: “I cannot run tools in this environment; this finding is hypothesis-only and requires runner/human verification.” Otherwise it may hallucinate measured d/S_k.

### Actively harmful to tool-decidability

1. **Conflict between §6 and §15 on d.** §6 says estimate d as analytical diversity; §15 says d must come from tool output. That is not merely expository; it creates inconsistent admissibility behaviour. Since core is off-limits, I would not reword here under this review, but the inconsistency should be flagged.

2. **“CLOSED … confirmed correctness” overclaim in §7.1.** Tool gates confirm only their coverage, not global correctness. This can cause models to under-challenge closed findings. Better would be “verified by configured pipeline,” but §7 is core-adjacent, so flag only.

3. **Historical/model-vote provenance in §18.** “Round-2 unanimous model review ratified…” is unnecessary and rhetically conflicts with the founding rule that model votes do not decide truth. Cut it.

4. **Future/provenance citations in §16.** The Hossenfelder/Vos anecdotes and date stamps invite present-day factual fragility and are not needed per turn. Keep the operational novelty rule, not the story.

## Q2 — Falsify the pruning method

The proposed lean-vs-full ablation is directionally sound, but the scoring metrics are too compliance-heavy. A cut can pass format compliance, R_k presence, FFAFP blocks, and alternatives supplied while quietly degrading:

- quality of falsifier construction,
- diversity of alternative hypotheses,
- willingness to withdraw weak claims,
- recognition of shared-prior convergence,
- proportionality judgment,
- quality of tool-invocation design,
- non-redundant exploration under low ρ / high γ.

Those are not captured by “block present” metrics. A model can satisfy the parser while emitting shallow falsification theatre.

Section-level ablation is also too coarse. The load-bearing unit is often a sentence or threshold, not a section. §18 is the clearest example: the Popper motivation and date-stamped provenance can go, but the contrast requirement, sibling isomorphism rule, and channel-assignment invariant probably cannot. If the entire section is removed and performance drops, the experiment only tells you “something in §18 mattered,” not which 900 chars were necessary.

Cross-section interactions matter too. §8.2 suspicious convergence reinforces the founding “not model votes” principle; §17 feedback reinforces §15 admissibility; §18 alternatives feed §16 η_int. Removing one may appear harmless until a task requires the coupled behaviour. Therefore the ablation set must include tasks targeting each interaction, not only ordinary code-review tasks.

Temp 0 and ≥2 runs are good for reproducibility but weak for behavioural robustness. At temp 0, you may only test one deterministic prompt trajectory per model. If the lean directive performs equally on that trajectory, it may still be more brittle under slight task wording changes. I would add prompt paraphrase perturbations rather than higher temperature: same ground truth, different surface form.

Cheaper/reliable method: first do **static directive minimisation** before model ablation. Convert each non-core section into atomic obligations:

- parser-required fields,
- validator thresholds,
- tool/human decision rules,
- registry/lifecycle rules,
- behavioural admonitions.

Then tag each sentence as one of: schema requirement, validator threshold, action rule, example, rationale, provenance, repetition. Delete only rationale/provenance/repetition first. That gives a lean candidate with high prior safety.

Then run ablation in three tiers:

1. **Parser compliance suite:** synthetic tasks checking required blocks.
2. **Ground-truth challenge suite:** known bugs/fixes where quality is objectively scored by tools.
3. **Adversarial reasoning suite:** duplicate findings, refuted feedback, closed findings, suspicious consensus, no-tool claims, alternative-isomorphism traps.

Use not just “block present,” but semantic/tool outcome metrics:

- falsifier executable or at least concretely runnable,
- tool receipt present,
- finding confirmed by hidden oracle,
- duplicate avoided,
- bad fix rejected below S*,
- refuted finding withdrawn or corrected,
- alternatives non-isomorphic by validator,
- no claim resolved by model agreement alone.

The per-model union restoration rule is good and appropriately conservative. My caveat: it may preserve too much if degradation is noise or task-specific. Require restoration only when degradation is reproducible on a targeted counterexample or exceeds a predeclared margin. Otherwise the directive will accrete forever.

My strongest likely disagreement with the panel: I would **not** cut §18 wholesale despite its size. It is bloated, but the alternative/contrast/isomorphism machinery is an operative anti-convergence mechanism, not mere motivational prose. The right move is a hard compression into validator-facing rules, not deletion.

VERDICT on the pruning method = SOUND-WITH-CAVEATS
CUT-LIST: section 13 Per-Round Operational Data; provenance/history paragraphs in sections 16, 17, and 18
COMPRESS-LIST: preamble ~300; 7.1 ~900; 8 ~500; 8.1 ~400; 8.2 ~600; 9 ~350; 10 ~250; 14 ~500; 16 ~2500; 17 ~1800; 18 ~4000
KEEP-VERBATIM: confirm the core stays untouched: sections 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 11, 12, and 15, including all founder-declared core formats, equations, definitions, gates, and tags
ONE-THING: the single highest-value prune is compressing §18 into a compact validator checklist while deleting its Popper motivation, ratification history, implementation provenance, and repeated orthogonality narration.
